l’homme surpasse l’homme — “Man surpasses man.” B. Pascal, Pensées (Brunschvicg), fragment 434.
“Si j’avais la disgrâce d’être Allemand …” — Correctly: “… les deux Bigs de ce temps-là — bigre de Bigs! — j’aurai été tenté …”
Henri Murger — (1822–1861), French writer whose novel Les scènes de la vie de bohème provided the basis for Puccini’s opera La Bohème.

**Henry Miller’s Tropique du Cancer*** — Here and in the quotations that follow, Schmitt is referring to Henry Miller, *Tropique du Cancer, translated by Paul Rivert, preface by Henri Fluchère, Paris 1945. Schmitt obtained the book, which did not appear in German until 1953, with Ernst Jünger’s help; see BW EJ, pp. 234–235.

Salus ex Judaeis — Vulgate, John 4:22: vos adoratis quod nescitis nos adoramus quod scimus quia salus ex Iudaeis est. “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation comes from the Jews.”

Bes uswika — Title of a poem by the Serbian poet Milutin Bojić (1892–1917), translated by Schmitt in 1923 together with his future wife Duška Todorović; see Tb 1921–24, pp. 203–204 and elsewhere. See also Carl Schmitt, “Illyrien — Notizen von einer dalmatinischen Reise,” in SGN, pp. 485–490.
the brilliant essay by Herbert Krüger — Herbert Krüger, “Das Janusgesicht der Nürnberger Prozesse,” in Die Gegenwart 3, 1948, no. 66, pp. 11 ff. See also Kempner’s reply, ibid., no. 68, pp. 9 ff.

in jus et favorem bellum justum gerentis — “… si iure belli factum est, omnia cedunt in favorem iustum bellum gerentis.” “If something has been done under the law of war, everything gives way in favor of those who wage a just war.”
“At last time turns Saul …” — From Johann Christian Günther’s poem “Trostaria”; J. Chr. Günther, Gesammelte Gedichte, ed. H. Heckmann, Munich 1981, pp. 291–292.
animus hostilis — hostile intent or disposition.
les êtres humains font une faune et une flore étranges … — Henry Miller, Tropique du Cancer, cited above, p. 349.

as Heraclitus says — “War is the father of all things and king of all things. Some he makes gods, others men; some slaves, others free.” Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, ed. Hermann Diels, Berlin 1903, p. 74, fragment 53.

Annie Kraus — (1900–1991), cousin of Georg Eisler, who had worked as Schmitt’s secretary in 1928–1929. Schmitt also went walking with her and visited cafés and cinemas with her. In his diary from this period he usually speaks positively of her, though he occasionally calls her “stupid.”

Kraus, who was also friends with Paul Adams and Eduard Rosenbaum, survived in Germany as a Jewish woman. She converted to Catholicism in 1942 and studied philosophy, among others, with Heidegger. See Andreas Mix, “Hilfe im katholischen Milieu,” in Überleben im Dritten Reich. Juden im Untergrund und ihre Helfer, ed. Wolfgang Benz, Munich 2003, pp. 131–142.
Her 1948 book Über die Dummheit, which is strongly influenced by Thomas Aquinas, says on p. 38:

“Freedom of the will takes shape through its bond with true Being, with God. When the will abandons this bond, there emerges the abstract un-boundness of arbitrary choice, which is therefore stupid in its very essence. The recent past has provided no shortage of drastic examples of this groundless ‘presence’ presenting itself as ‘the existential’ (Carl Schmitt).”

“Sin begins in the mind: all these intellectually gifted creators of heretical philosophical doctrines bear a profound share of responsibility for the final degradation of their people—a degradation that may even surprise them themselves, so thoroughly have they already become ‘stupid’ …”

In 1983 Annie Kraus helped bring about a reconciliation between Schmitt and Georg Eisler. See Reinhard Mehring, “Annie Kraus, der Würgeengel des Carl Schmitt,” in FAZ, 20 July 2007, p. 35; and Mehring, Die Hamburger Verlegerfamilie Eisler und Carl Schmitt (Plettenberger Miniaturen, 2), Plettenberg 2009, pp. 18 and 27–28.
Con-versanti in re illicita / co-existentibus in re illicita — “Those who together find themselves in evil circumstances must live together in evil circumstances.” See the note above on p. 148.
at Ostermann’s — An inn in Plettenberg-Eiringhausen.
“The serpent, it is said …” — Jeremy Bentham, The Works of J. Bentham, Edinburgh 1838, vol. 1, part 2, p. 325.

protestatio factis et actis contraria — Refers to the following rule of Roman law: protestatio facto contraria non valet. A reservation or declaration has no validity if it contradicts one’s own actual conduct.
“l’obscurité protège mieux que la loi” — Rivarol: “We live in an age in which obscurity protects better than the law and gives greater reassurance than innocence.”

Schmitt did not begin quoting this maxim only after his exclusion from academic life. He had already used it during his period of service in the Volkssturm. He and Jünger discussed at length how obscurité should be translated.
Jünger initially proposed “Nichtigkeit” (“insignificance” or “nothingness”), then “Niedrigkeit” (“lowliness”), both of which Schmitt rejected. See BW EJ, pp. 279–292.

Jünger eventually translated the maxim as: “We live in an age in which insignificance offers more protection than the laws and gives a better conscience than innocence.” E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 14, p. 274.

Even this probably did not capture what Schmitt understood Rivarol to mean. Jünger discussed the difficulty of translating obscurité in the appendix to his Rivarol edition, cited above, pp. 322 ff. See also BW Forsthoff, p. 114.
Bible de l’humanité — Jules Michelet, Bible de l’humanité, Paris 1864.
The Yogi and the Commissar — Arthur Koestler, Der Yogi und der Kommissar. Auseinandersetzungen, Esslingen 1950.

Nohl, pp. 347–348 — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Hegels theologische Jugendschriften, edited from the manuscripts in the Royal Library in Berlin by Dr. Herman Nohl, Tübingen 1907. A copy survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265, no. 24647.
“For as thou urgest justice be assured …” — Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act IV, Scene 1.
Ave consilescens in arcano — “Greetings, fellow keeper of silence in the secret.”
the pack of Korah — Korah and his followers rose in rebellion against Moses; Numbers 16–17.
“So Christ has already been dead for our sins for so long …” — Quoted in Karl Rosenkranz, G. W. F. Hegels Leben, facsimile reprint of the Berlin 1844 edition, Darmstadt 1969, p. 541.

is supposed to become Lukács’s star witness (Lukács, p. 590) — Georg Lukács, Der junge Hegel. Über die Beziehungen von Dialektik und Oekonomie, Zurich and Vienna 1948, p. 590. A copy survives in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265, no. 24641.
news of poor Gustav Adolf Walz’s death — Walz, who had been dismissed from his university position in 1945 and interned by the French occupying authorities, died on 17 December 1948.
On 10 January 1949 Schmitt wrote to E. R. Huber:
“Will anyone have the courage to do justice to Walz in public? […] This is how we are being finished off—Walz at fifty.”
Ecce quomodo moritur iustus, et nemo considerat — “Behold how the just man dies, and no one takes notice.” From the medieval liturgy for the death of John the Baptist.

but I will remember him — The depth of Schmitt’s reaction to the death of his colleague can be seen from the fact that he still commemorated Walz in his speech on his sixty-fifth birthday in 1953; see Schmittiana NF II, 2014, p. 291.
Konrad Weiß — The quotations that follow are from Weiß’s drama Konradin von Hohenstaufen.
William Ebenstein — (1910–1976), Austrian-American political scientist. Schmitt believed that Ebenstein had misrepresented him in his book Man and the State (New York 1947); see BW Mohler, p. 25.
Le combat spirituel est plus brutal que la bataille des homes — Correctly:
Le combat spirituel est aussi brutal que la bataille d’hommes; mais la vision de la justice est le plaisir de Dieu seul.
“The spiritual struggle is as brutal as battle between men; but the vision of justice is God’s pleasure alone.”
Arthur Rimbaud, Sämtliche Dichtungen. Französisch und Deutsch, ed. and trans. Walther Küchler, 6th ed., Heidelberg 1982, p. 324.
“Now the laws, seen through to their primal depths, will shatter” — Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht (Geneva edition), vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, poem “Neumond,” p. 544.
Gottfried Benn: “I am not of the opinion …” — Gottfried Benn, Drei alte Männer, in Sämtliche Werke, vol. VII/1, Stuttgart 2003, p. 121; first published in Wiesbaden in 1949.

Etat postiche — “artificial” or “fake state.” Schmitt probably borrowed the term from Georges Sorel, Réflexions sur la violence (Études sur le devenir social, 4), 4th ed., Paris 1919. Schmitt’s annotated copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 25175.
To Mrs. Jünger — See BW GJ, pp. 112 ff.
on the subject of Chaopolites — Schmitt wrote to Ernst Jünger on 25 November 1949: “As you know, I am a Chaopolite, not a Heliopolite.” BW EJ, p. 241.

**the Ludus de Antichristo*** — Schmitt is referring to the following edition: Gottfried Hasenkamp, ed., *Das Spiel vom Antichrist, translated into German with an afterword on the Ludus de Antichristo, its performance, and its translation, Münster 1932. Schmitt’s copy, with a dedication from the editor, survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 24532.
“In the spell of this luxuriant paradise-air …” — Correctly:
“In the spell of luxuriant paradisal delight, every claim upon life and every hope for the hereafter finds satisfaction.”

Johann Jakob Bachofen, Der Mythus von Orient und Occident. Eine Metaphysik der Alten Welt, with an introduction by Alfred Baeumler, ed. Manfred Schroeter, Munich 1926, p. 402. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265, no. 24846.
“A scarcely greeted, lost, unspeakable moment” — Nikolaus Lenau, poem “Frage,” in Lenau, Sämtliche Werke und Briefe, vol. 1, Frankfurt am Main and Leipzig 1970, p. 120:
“Human heart, what is your happiness? A moment born as a mystery, scarcely greeted and already lost, never to be repeated!”

En quelque façon nul … — See Hans Peter Ipsen, “Deutsche Gerichtsbarkeit unter Besatzungsmacht (Einwirkungen der Besatzung auf den gerichtlichen Rechtsschutz gegen deutsche Hoheitsakte in der britischen Besatzungszone),” in Festschrift zu Ehren von Prof. Dr. jur. Rudolf Laun, Rektor der Universität Hamburg, 1948, pp. 68–96.
Schmitt discusses Montesquieu’s formula, which referred to the judiciary, in his Verfassungslehre; VL, pp. 184–185.
Venire contra factum proprium — “To act contrary to one’s own previous conduct”; a formula from German law of obligations.
Rolf Stödter in his otherwise very thorough book — Rolf Stödter, Deutschlands Rechtslage, Hamburg 1948.

C. M. O. van Nispen tot Sevenaer — Carel Marie Otto van Nispen tot Sevenaer, L’occupation allemande pendant la dernière guerre mondiale. Considerations sur le caractère du pouvoir de la puissance occupante et de ses mesures selon les principes généraux du droit et selon la 4e convention de La Haye, The Hague 1946.
Barandon’s Hamburg radio lecture — Paul Barandon (1881–1971), German diplomat who at this time was a private lecturer in international law at the University of Hamburg.
Otto Veit, speeches — 29. Dezember 1948. Ansprachen von Ernst Beutler und Otto Veit, Frankfurt am Main 1948, commemorative publication for Otto Veit’s fiftieth birthday.
“In you I see the God …” — Stefan George, “Kunfttag,” in George, Werke. Ausgabe in zwei Bänden, 3rd ed., Düsseldorf and Munich 1976, vol. 1, p. 279. Correctly: “… whom I recognized with a shudder …”

Kurt Hiller’s enemy-flailing — Kurt Hiller (1885–1972), pacifist writer. Schmitt regarded his article “Ewiger Friede in Gänsefüßchen” (Die Weltbühne, year 28, 4 October 1932, pp. 498–500) as “one of the many examples of documentary value in which the word and concept ‘annihilation’ are attributed to me”; BW Mohler, p. 48.
against Paetel — Karl Otto Paetel (1906–1975), writer and leading representative of National Bolshevism.
“The men of the German National Assembly in Frankfurt …” — Quotation from Bruno Bauer. Correctly:
